planting.note: Plant corms deep in fall next to an existing shrub or a few stout brush stakes so the twining flower scape has something to climb; without support the stems sprawl untidily.

directions: The only geophyte in this group with a twining habit, this species' weak flower scape coils up through shrub branches to display a dense pink umbel several feet off the ground — a genuine conversation piece and a way to grow a bulb vertically without a trellis. Corms self-bury, setting themselves progressively deeper each year, so dig deep if transplanting. Give it dilute liquid fertilizer during the active winter-spring growth phase to improve bloom size, then keep it bone dry in summer like other California corms.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall at the front edge of a dry bed or on bare gravelly ground where taller grassland companions won't shade it out; its flowers sit almost at ground level.

directions: One of the shortest brodiaeas, this species flowers almost at ground level, making it a true rock-garden or trough geophyte rather than a border plant. It tolerates both full sun and the light shade of its native coastal bluff and prairie habitat. Skip this one for containers meant to be admired at eye level — it's a plant for kneeling down to appreciate.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in gravelly-clay, open grassland conditions; slightly richer soil than its smaller relatives tolerate rewards heavier bloom and taller stems.

directions: The largest-flowered common Brodiaea, blooming to about two inches across, this species is taller and showier than the already-common harvest and elegant brodiaeas, and makes a reliable cut flower. Give it the gravelly-clay, open grassland conditions it uses in the wild. Because it's a late bloomer, often flowering into summer in some populations, it extends the Brodiaea flowering season in a mixed native-bulb planting.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall tucked among chaparral shrubs or on thin, rocky soil where competition is low, rather than in a rich bed.

directions: A diminutive, chaparral-adapted companion for rock gardens and dry-bank plantings where larger brodiaeas would be out of scale, this species carries distinct staminode and stamen structure giving interesting flower detail even at small size. Best used the way it grows in nature — tucked among chaparral shrubs or on thin, rocky soil where competition is low. Its common name 'Chaparral Brodiaea' distinguishes it from the similarly-named Dwarf Brodiaea in the collection.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall at the edge of a seasonal swale or in a meadow mix that stays damp into late spring, not a scree bed; pot young seedlings and grow on a year or two before planting out.

directions: Flowers held on extraordinarily long pedicels up to seven inches produce a loose, firework-like umbel unlike the tight clusters of other Triteleia, and this species is unusual in tolerating vernally moist ground such as meadows and vernal-pool margins. Unlike the gravelly-slope bulbs in this collection, it wants a spot that stays damp into late spring rather than a scree bed. First-year corms are small and slow, so pot up young seedling bulbs and grow on for a year or two before planting into permanent positions.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall on dry, rocky, heavier-textured soil matching its bluff and open-woods habitat rather than loose sandy ground.

directions: Lavender-blue, dark-veined funnel flowers distinguish this species, restricted to dry rocky bluffs and open woods of the northern California Coast Ranges and Sierra foothills, adding a distinct regional ecotype beyond the already-present coastal Triteleia species. This species forms new daughter corms stacked above the old one each year, so when dividing or transplanting, dig deeper than expected and anticipate finding a small vertical chain of corms rather than a single bulb. Site on dry, rocky, heavier-textured soil to match its native habitat.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in a trough or raised rock garden with sharp drainage; in hot-summer gardens outside its native range, give afternoon shade rather than full baking sun.

directions: One of the only yellow-flowered Triteleia species — most of the genus runs blue, violet, or white — this species fills a real color gap for a native-bulb rock garden palette. Because it comes from higher, cooler elevations in the Klamath Mountains, give it sharper drainage and don't assume it needs the same hot, bone-dry summer baking as lowland Triteleia. Its small stature suits troughs and raised rock gardens better than open beds.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall as a true dry-gravel or rock-outcrop plant; within its native range it needs no summer irrigation at all once established.

directions: Unusual yellow-or-white flowers with a dark purple-brown midvein and contrasting blue anthers give this species a distinctive color combination not found in any other Triteleia in the collection. Within its native Klamath-Siskiyou range it needs no summer irrigation at all once established, so treat it as a true dry-gravel or rock-outcrop plant rather than a border bulb. It is more commonly available through Pacific Northwest native-seed specialists than through California nurseries.
